description: Strings track: 4 lessons, 10 knowledge checks, 5 practice problems.

coding.title: Reverse a String
coding.problemStatement: Given a string s consisting of lowercase letters, print the string reversed.
coding.inputFormat: A single line containing the string s.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters

coding.title: Character Frequency
coding.problemStatement:
You are given a string of lowercase English letters. For every letter that appears in it, print the letter and how many times it appears, in alphabetical order.

One pass with a 26-slot counting array (or a dictionary) is enough — no sorting of the string needed.
coding.inputFormat: A single line containing the string s.
coding.outputFormat: One line per distinct letter, in alphabetical order: the letter, a space, and its count.
constraints: s contains only lowercase letters a-z

examples.explanation: 'a' appears 3 times, 'b' once and 'n' twice; letters are listed alphabetically.

coding.title: Reverse the Words in a Sentence
coding.problemStatement:
You are given a line of text containing words separated by one or more spaces. It may also have spaces at the start or end. Print the words in reverse order, separated by exactly one space.

A "word" is any run of non-space characters. The characters inside each word keep their order — only the order of the words changes.
coding.inputFormat: A single line of text containing at least one word.
coding.outputFormat: The words in reverse order, separated by single spaces, with no leading or trailing spaces.
constraints: Words contain letters and digits only
There is at least one word

examples.explanation: The double space between "sky" and "is" collapses to one space in the output.

coding.problemStatement:
You are given n words. Find the longest string that every word starts with. If the words have no common prefix, print a single dash (-).

Compare the words column by column: the prefix ends at the first position where a word runs out or two words disagree.
coding.inputFormat: First line: an integer n. Each of the next n lines: one word.
coding.outputFormat: The longest common prefix, or - if it is empty.

mcqs.title: Strings check: indexing characters
mcqs.explanation: Strings are indexed like arrays: `s[0]` is "h", `s[4]` is "o". `s[-1]` also means the last character, "o".

mcqs.title: Strings check: immutability
mcqs.questionText: In Python, what happens when this runs?
mcqs.explanation: Python (and Java) strings are immutable. To "change" one you build a new string, e.g. `s = "j" + s[1:]`.

options.optionText: It raises a TypeError — strings cannot be changed in place
It creates a new string automatically

mcqs.title: Strings check: building a string in a loop
mcqs.questionText: You build a string of n characters by doing `result = result + ch` inside a loop. Why is collecting the characters in a list and calling `"".join(...)` once usually better?
mcqs.explanation: Because strings are immutable, `result + ch` creates a new string and copies everything built so far. Over n steps that is 1 + 2 + … + n = O(n²) copying. Collecting pieces and joining once is O(n). In Java, use a StringBuilder for the same reason.

options.optionText: Each `+` copies the whole string so far, so the loop can cost O(n²); join builds it once in O(n)
`+` does not work with single characters
There is no difference in cost

mcqs.title: Strings check: counting array index
mcqs.questionText: With a 26-slot counting array for lowercase letters, which index stores the count of the letter c held in `ch`?
mcqs.explanation: Subtracting the code of 'a' maps 'a'→0, 'b'→1, …, 'z'→25 — exactly the 26 slots. `ord(ch)` alone would be around 97–122 and overflow a 26-slot array.

mcqs.title: Strings check: array or dictionary
mcqs.questionText: You need to count characters in a string that may contain any Unicode character. Which is the better counter?
mcqs.explanation: A 26-slot array only works when the alphabet is known and small (like a–z). For arbitrary characters a dictionary grows to fit whatever appears, still O(n) overall. Sorting costs O(n log n); pairwise comparison is O(n²).

options.optionText: A dictionary (hash map) keyed by character
Sorting the string first, then counting
A nested loop comparing every pair of characters

mcqs.title: Strings check: split with extra spaces
mcqs.explanation: `split()` with no argument splits on any run of whitespace and drops leading/trailing whitespace, so you get just the words. `split(" ")` would keep the empty strings between repeated spaces.

mcqs.title: Strings check: join
mcqs.explanation: `reversed(words)` yields "c", "b", "a", and `"-".join(...)` puts the separator between them.

mcqs.title: Strings check: two pointers for palindromes
mcqs.questionText: Checking whether a string of length n is a palindrome with one pointer at each end: when can you stop and answer "not a palindrome"?
mcqs.explanation: A palindrome needs every mirrored pair to match, so the first mismatch proves it is not one. Otherwise move both pointers inward until they meet: at most n/2 comparisons and O(1) extra space.

options.optionText: As soon as the characters at the two pointers differ
Only after comparing all n characters
When the pointers are next to each other
Never — you must reverse the string first

mcqs.title: Strings check: longest common prefix
mcqs.questionText: Scanning n words column by column for their longest common prefix, which condition ends the prefix?
mcqs.explanation: The prefix must be a prefix of every word, so it stops at the first column where any word has run out of characters or the words disagree.

options.optionText: Some word ends, or two words have different characters in this column
The first word ends — the others do not matter

mcqs.title: Strings check: prefix trace
mcqs.explanation: Comparing "interview" with "internet" keeps "inter" (they differ at "v" vs "n"); "interval" also starts with "inter", so the prefix stays "inter".
mcqs.codeSnippet:
words = ["interview", "internet", "interval"]
prefix = words[0]
for w in words[1:]:
    i = 0
    while i < len(prefix) and i < len(w) and prefix[i] == w[i]:
        i += 1
    prefix = prefix[:i]
print(prefix or "-")

lessons.title: Strings: characters, indexing and immutability
lessons.summary: A string is a sequence of characters — index it like an array, but build new strings instead of editing in place.
objectives: Read individual characters and slices of a string by index
Explain why Python and Java strings cannot be changed in place
Build strings efficiently instead of with repeated `+` in a loop
lessons.concept:
A **string** is an ordered sequence of characters. Everything you learned about array indexing applies: the first character is at index `0`, the last at `len(s) - 1`, and reading `s[i]` is O(1).

```python
s = "binary"
print(s[0])      # b
print(s[-1])     # y  — negative indices count from the end
print(s[1:4])    # ina — a slice: indices 1, 2 and 3
```

## Strings are immutable

In Python and Java you **cannot change a character in place**. `s[0] = "B"` is an error. Every "change" creates a new string:

```python
s = "binary"
s = "B" + s[1:]   # a brand-new string "Binary"
```

(C++ `std::string` is mutable — `s[0] = 'B'` works there.)

## Why that matters for performance

Because each `+` builds a new string, appending one character at a time in a loop copies everything built so far, over and over — **O(n²)** for n characters. Instead, collect the pieces and join them once, which is **O(n)**:

```python
pieces = []
for ch in "binary":
    pieces.append(ch.upper())
result = "".join(pieces)   # "BINARY"
```

In Java, use a `StringBuilder` for the same reason.
lessons.example:
Reversing a string three ways — all O(n):

```python
s = "stressed"

print(s[::-1])                 # desserts — slice with step -1
print("".join(reversed(s)))    # desserts

chars = []
for i in range(len(s) - 1, -1, -1):
    chars.append(s[i])
print("".join(chars))          # desserts
```

And in C++, where strings are mutable, you can reverse in place with two indices:

```cpp
string s = "stressed";
int i = 0, j = s.size() - 1;
while (i < j) swap(s[i++], s[j--]);
cout << s << "\n";  // desserts
```
lessons.commonMistakes:
- **Trying to assign into a Python/Java string.** `s[i] = x` fails; build a new string or work on a list of characters.
- **Concatenating inside a long loop.** Fine for a handful of pieces, but O(n²) for large inputs — collect and `join`.
- **Forgetting the newline when reading input.** `input()` strips it in Python; in C++ mixing `cin >>` with `getline` can leave a stray newline — read consistently.

lessons.title: Counting characters
lessons.summary: Count how often each character appears in one pass — with a fixed-size array or a dictionary.
objectives: Map a lowercase letter to an array slot with `ord(ch) - ord('a')`
Count characters in one O(n) pass
Choose between a counting array and a dictionary
lessons.concept:
Many string problems start with **how many times does each character appear?** — anagrams, the most frequent letter, whether two strings use the same letters. Visiting each character once and incrementing a counter answers it in **O(n)**.

## A counting array (small, known alphabet)

For lowercase English letters there are only 26 possibilities, so a 26-slot array is enough. Map each letter to a slot by subtracting the code of `'a'`:

```python
counts = [0] * 26
for ch in "banana":
    counts[ord(ch) - ord("a")] += 1
# counts[0] == 3 (a), counts[1] == 1 (b), counts[13] == 2 (n)
```

Printing the non-zero slots in index order gives the letters **alphabetically**, with no sorting.

## A dictionary (any characters)

When the characters could be anything — capitals, digits, punctuation, Unicode — use a dictionary (hash map). It only stores the characters that actually appear:

```python
counts = {}
for ch in "Hello, World!":
    counts[ch] = counts.get(ch, 0) + 1
```

Both approaches are one pass, O(n) time. The array uses a fixed 26 slots; the dictionary uses space proportional to the number of *distinct* characters.
lessons.commonMistakes:
- **Indexing by the raw character code.** `counts[ord(ch)]` needs ~123 slots; subtract `ord('a')` to land in 0–25.
- **Using a 26-slot array for mixed input.** Capitals or digits fall outside 0–25 and crash or corrupt counts — use a dictionary, or normalise first (`ch.lower()`).
- **Sorting to count.** Sorting works but costs O(n log n); a single counting pass is O(n).

lessons.title: Splitting, joining and parsing words
lessons.summary: Turn a line of text into words and back again — and handle messy spacing correctly.
objectives: Split a line into words, including lines with repeated or surrounding spaces
Join words back together with a chosen separator
Reverse, filter or reorder words without touching the characters inside them
lessons.concept:
Text input often arrives as a single line of words. Two operations do most of the work: **split** the line into a list of words, and **join** a list back into one string.

## Splitting

With no arguments, Python's `split()` splits on **any run of whitespace** and ignores spaces at the start and end:

```python
"  the sky  is blue ".split()     # ['the', 'sky', 'is', 'blue']
```

Passing a separator is stricter — every single space counts, so repeated spaces produce empty strings:

```python
"the sky  is".split(" ")          # ['the', 'sky', '', 'is']
```

For "words separated by spaces", the no-argument form is almost always what you want.

## Joining

`separator.join(words)` puts the separator **between** items — never at the ends:

```python
" ".join(["blue", "is", "sky"])   # 'blue is sky'
", ".join(["a", "b", "c"])        # 'a, b, c'
```

## Working with words

Once the line is a list, it's just array work: reverse it, filter it, sort it, count it — then join the result. Splitting and joining are both O(n) in the length of the line.
lessons.commonMistakes:
- **`split(" ")` on messy input.** It keeps empty strings for repeated spaces; use `split()` unless every separator is exactly one space.
- **Building the output with a trailing separator.** Printing `word + " "` in a loop leaves a space at the end; `join` never does.
- **Reversing the characters instead of the words.** `line[::-1]` reverses letters too — split first, reverse the list, then join.

lessons.title: Two pointers and prefixes on strings
lessons.summary: Compare characters from both ends or column by column — palindromes and common prefixes in linear time.
objectives: Check a palindrome with two pointers in O(n) time and O(1) extra space
Stop early as soon as a comparison fails
Find the longest common prefix of several words by scanning columns
lessons.concept:
Two techniques from arrays carry straight over to strings.

## Two pointers from both ends

A string is a **palindrome** when it reads the same forwards and backwards. Put one pointer at each end and walk them toward the middle:

```python
def is_palindrome(s):
    i, j = 0, len(s) - 1
    while i < j:
        if s[i] != s[j]:
            return False     # first mismatch settles it
        i += 1
        j -= 1
    return True
```

At most `n / 2` comparisons — O(n) time — and no copy of the string, so O(1) extra space. Compare that with `s == s[::-1]`, which is also O(n) but builds a reversed copy.

## Scanning columns: the longest common prefix

For several words, the longest common prefix is the part every word starts with. Keep a candidate prefix and shorten it against each word:

```python
def common_prefix(words):
    prefix = words[0]
    for w in words[1:]:
        i = 0
        while i < len(prefix) and i < len(w) and prefix[i] == w[i]:
            i += 1
        prefix = prefix[:i]
    return prefix
```

The prefix ends at the first column where a word **runs out** or the characters **disagree**. The total work is bounded by the total number of characters.
lessons.example:
Tracing the common prefix of `["flower", "flow", "flight"]`:

| word | compared with | matching part | prefix after |
|---|---|---|---|
| flow | flower | `flow` | flow |
| flight | flow | `fl` (o ≠ i) | fl |

Result: `fl`. With `["dog", "car"]` the first letters differ, so the prefix is empty.
lessons.commonMistakes:
- **Comparing past the end of a shorter word.** Always check `i < len(w)` before `w[i]`.
- **Forgetting the empty result.** When nothing is shared the prefix is `""` — decide how to print it (this platform's problems ask for `-`).
- **Moving only one pointer.** In the palindrome check both pointers must move inward every step, or the loop never ends.
